title: Crypto and ICO scams: who really holds the money
body_md:
## A rising number is not a balance

The dashboard says your balance grew again overnight. That figure is whatever the site chooses to show, and it is no evidence that assets exist. A blockchain transfer can be traced, but once it is confirmed a bank normally cannot reverse it.

“Crypto” covers several different tricks: a fake exchange, a token whose insiders control the supply or the rules of sale, a coordinated price pump, an upfront fee for “recovering” lost funds. Keep them apart. None of this makes every crypto asset a fraud.

### Four questions before the first deposit

Ask **who controls your funds, which legal entity offers the service, what produces the return, and what you can verify without the promoter’s help.** Read the withdrawal terms before you deposit anything. Stop if an acquaintance you know only online picks the platform, promises steady high returns or asks you to send money to a personal wallet. An ad in a respected outlet or a celebrity’s photo is distribution, not due diligence. And a tiny first withdrawal may be allowed on purpose, to earn your trust.

### Presales, registers and the limits of a license

For a token presale or initial coin offering (ICO), look for a documented project, a clear allocation of tokens, the privileges written into the contract and, where one exists, an independent technical review. Even an audit cannot guarantee a price or honesty. If a financial firm stands behind the pitch, look it up in the relevant regulator’s register for its actual activity, not just a matching name. The Bank of Russia’s register covers specified financial activities in Russia; it does not validate an overseas platform, and it promises no return.

### A bad bet is not a scam

A sound but volatile investment can lose money without any fraud. A legitimate exchange can also ask for identity checks under its own rules. What gives the game away is an unexpected demand to pay a separate “tax” into an unfamiliar wallet before your balance is released. Do not send extra money to test it. If you have been hurt, keep the dates, transaction hashes and addresses somewhere private, contact the exchange or the payment provider promptly and report it to the proper authority. Ignore recovery agents who approach you unasked.

widget_config.goal: Tell a checkable offer from a fake platform or a token pitch, before any money is sent.
widget_config.today_action: Before you follow any investment link, write four lines: the exact legal entity, who holds the assets, where the return comes from and which regulator covers it. A blank line means no deposit.
widget_config.scope: Educational risk checks, not investment advice. The US sources (FBI, FTC, SEC) and the Russian register belong to different jurisdictions; checked 2026-10-20. The examples are invented.

blocks.title: The presale with no way out
blocks.situation: A group promotes `orbit-seed.example` with a fixed monthly return. The token chart climbs. The terms never say who holds the deposits, and the contract lets its creator block sales.
blocks.analysis: A chart on the site proves neither real trades nor a real market. With no named custodian and a contract the creator can use to block sales, you cannot price the risk, and a promised fixed return makes it worse. Do not deposit. Look up the entity, the contract and any regulatory status on your own.

blocks.title: A real platform that checks who you are
blocks.situation: You reach a licensed provider through a bookmark you saved long ago. Its published terms warn that a withdrawal after a large transaction may need an identity review inside the app. It asks for no payment from outside.
blocks.analysis: An identity review is not automatically a scam. Check the exact legal entity and licensed activity with the relevant regulator, contact support from the site you reached yourself, and never send documents in a DM. A license lowers one kind of doubt and leaves market risk untouched.

blocks.title: A stranger’s token tip
blocks.setup: An invented chat: a stranger in a hobby group offers access to a new token and an “expert” trading site. You have not sent any money.

steps.prompt: They send a screenshot of a rising balance. What do you ask first?

choices.text: Who controls the funds, and what independently confirms the trading firm?
choices.consequence: You find that every piece of evidence comes from the promoter.
choices.explanation: A screenshot is easy to fake. Ask about ownership and authority.

choices.text: Take the rising chart as proof of profit.
choices.consequence: You may be mistaking a stage-managed screen for real assets.
choices.explanation: A profit on a screen is not money you can withdraw.

steps.prompt: A search turns up a registered company with a similar name. What now?

choices.text: Transfer the money, since any register match means it is safe.
choices.consequence: The recipient could be an impostor, or the product could fall outside the license.
choices.explanation: Match the entity and the activity, not only the brand.

choices.text: Match the exact legal entity, domain and licensed activity in the relevant register.
choices.consequence: A matching name no longer carries the decision on its own.
choices.explanation: A real company can be impersonated, and a license has a defined scope.

steps.prompt: The promoter points to a tiny withdrawal as proof that the site is sound. Whether or not you sent money in the last step, what about further transfers?

choices.text: Send a larger sum to see whether that comes back too.
choices.consequence: Another payment is exposed, whether or not you had sent money before.
choices.explanation: A bigger deposit is not a way to test a platform.

choices.text: Stop sending; if you have already paid, contact the service you paid through right away.
choices.consequence: No new transfer goes out. Money already sent stays exposed; the service can look at the options but cannot promise recovery.
choices.explanation: A controlled platform can pay back a little to draw in a lot. Stopping now does not undo an earlier transfer.

steps.prompt: A separate case: someone who already sent money to this platform gets an unsolicited DM from a “recovery specialist” demanding a fee up front. What should they do?

choices.text: Refuse to pay; keep the evidence and go to the provider and the official reporting routes.
choices.consequence: They avoid a second loss and keep their records.
choices.explanation: IC3 warns specifically about upfront fees for “recovery.”

choices.text: Pay, because the specialist knows the transaction hash.
choices.consequence: Anyone can copy public ledger data, and paying adds another loss.
choices.explanation: Knowing a hash proves no authority to recover anything.

blocks.debrief: These checks decided it: who receives the money, who controls it, which activity is regulated and what the withdrawal terms really say. Even once a genuine firm is identified, risk remains. Go through it again and take the tempting turn once, to see where it leads.

questions.prompt: A token contract displays an audit badge. What follows?

choices.text: The investment cannot fall in value.
choices.explanation: An audit leaves market risk and liquidity risk exactly where they were.

choices.text: Read the audit’s scope; it cannot guarantee a price or honesty.
choices.explanation: An audit covers a defined piece of code, not every business or market risk.

questions.prompt: A Russian register lists a firm with a similar name. How should you read that?

choices.text: Check the exact identity and the authorized activity; do not infer returns.
choices.explanation: The register has a defined jurisdiction and scope of activity.

choices.text: Every crypto product in the world is certified.
choices.explanation: A Russian register cannot certify the world.

questions.prompt: A platform demands a separate wallet transfer before it releases your profits. What do you do?

choices.text: Pay once, since the displayed balance is bigger than the fee.
choices.explanation: The displayed balance may be fiction, and fees can keep coming.

choices.text: Stop paying, keep your records, and contact the provider and the authorities.
choices.explanation: Extra payments to “release” a balance are a known fraud pattern.
